newsitem.title: CHINA: Deng set stage for recovery of Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Deng set stage for recovery of Hong Kong.

text.p: Deng Xiaoping went to meet Mao Zedong and other late communist mentors bearing one trophy they never obtained: the recovery of Hong Kong from the British in 1997.

"It is a matter of great pride for Deng that he, unlike Mao or Zhou Enlai, has been able to obtain the promise of the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule in 1997," wrote David Goodman and Gerald Segal in a 1995 monograph "China Without Deng".

Such was Deng's satisfaction in solving that vexing matter of national pride that family members quoted him as saying he refused to die before July 1, 1997, when Hong Kong would take down the British Union Jack and hoist China's five-star flag.
Hong Kong's return owes as much to the calendar -- the British lease on Hong Kong's New Territories was to run out in 1997 -- as to Deng's diplomatic policies.

But the achievement of Deng, who set the broad strategy for the colony's return and left the specifics to others, was to lay the framework that would enable capitalist Hong Kong -- and eventually Taiwan, he hoped -- to exist within communist China.
Deng called his policy "one country, two systems".

"This means that within the People's Republic of China, the mainland with its 1.2 billion people will maintain the socialist system, while Hong Kong and Taiwan continue under the capitalist system," Deng explained in 1984.
Deng, who won wide admiration for economic reforms that scrapped Mao's crude autarchy and raised China's standard of living, won fresh plaudits for political pragmatism.

"Deng must be credited with having come up with an imaginative concept to resolve the dilemmas inherent in the problems of reuniting both Hong Kong and Taiwan," wrote British Sinologist Michael Yahuda in "Deng Xiaoping: Portrait of a Chinese Statesman".

Deng's pragmatism reassured sceptics in Hong Kong, many of whose residents fled Communist rule, that he was serious about his pledge to maintain the British colony's social, economic and legal systems.

"When we adopt the policy of 'one country, two systems' to resolve the Hong Kong question, we are not acting on impulse or playing tricks but are proceeding from reality and taking into full account the past and present circumstances of Hong Kong," he told prominent figures from the colony.
Five years after the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration formalising the transfer of Hong Kong was signed, however, it was the circumstances of China that had changed.

The slaying of pro-democracy protesters in Beijing in June 1989, ordered by Deng, put a freeze on expanding liberties in China and chilled Hong Kong, which had grown more politically aware after the Tiananmen crackdown.

To an administration made paranoid by the turmoil of June 1989 and the collapse of European communism several months later, "one-country, two systems" became a recipe for Hong Kong subversion of the socialist mainland.
China's response was heavy-handed bulldozer diplomacy that sought to browbeat London and Hong Kong into abandoning modest democratic reforms introduced in the early 1990s.
The result in Hong Kong was diminished confidence as the colony of 6.3 million people faced an uncertain future as a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China.

Less than 500 days before the transfer, the Chinese-language Hong Kong Economic Journal said Beijing's clumsy handling of a local religious issue showed that China's habit of "picking up a rock, only to drop it on its own foot" had died hard.
The tough line of Deng's successors at home and towards Hong Kong militated against the other aim of the one country, two systems approach -- recovering the rebel province of Taiwan.

"The crudeness of Chinese policy in Hong Kong is part of the reason for China's gradual loss of Taiwan," wrote Segal and Goodman, adding that Taiwan's democratic reforms had made China's embrace less appealing despite closer economic ties.

"Deng believed that opening up China to Taiwan would bring the two closer together. Instead, it has convinced even those on Taiwan who were somewhat nationalistically sympathetic to the mainland that reunification is both unlikely and unnecessary," the authors said.
Deng's words on reunification with Taiwan in 1984 carried China's conviction that reunification was inevitable, if a time-consuming process.
"If it cannot be accomplished in 100 years it will be in 1,000 years," he said.
